scenario: WIBTA for kicking my girlfriends older sister out of our apartment? | Apologies in advance. This is a really long story. I’ve lived with my girlfriend for 2 years. We moved to the apartment we are at now a year ago. We used to live with her sister and another couple. We’ll call my girlfriend L and her sister J. We moved because J would always have people over , and we wanted the privacy of no roommates. Once we moved, someone took our spot there. Fast forward from when we left (May 2018) to January 1st, 2020. J fucked her roommates over by not paying the rent for two months, as our landlords just accepted cash. For two months, she took the $3000 spent it on “bills” that her sister isn’t even sure about. After ruining her relationship with her roommates, She got the money from family to pay the rent off, and asked L and I to move in until the end of January. Her uncle would pick her up and she’d move out of state. She basically never asked the uncle to come get her, mentioned to L that she might just stay in New York. My girlfriend, who isn’t confrontational, never opposed her living with us for free. So J has been with us for about 4 months, no job, just contributing sometimes with cooking. She only comes here to sleep after she parties with her friends. Our house is essentially a hangover den. What makes matters worse is because of the current situation, the job she had a chance at has shut down. So shes not even looking for work. But that isn’t stopping her from going out every other night, to parties, where she doesn’t even think that if she was to get sick from being stupid, it would affect us as well. L wants her out, but is really conflicted because it’s her sister. I don’t think she’d be happy about me speaking to J about it, even though she also wants J out. I don’t want to seem like a dick, but it’s at the point where I might just take the risk of L being mad at me. I want my home back. I’ve been trying to get L to talk to her, but she just hates confrontation. I think I might just have to tell J if she doesn’t find a job to fund her getting her own place, she needs to to back to her mothers. WIBTA?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This is a **complicated and emotionally charged** situation, and your frustration is completely understandable—you’re dealing with a roommate who’s taking advantage of your girlfriend’s generosity while disrupting your living space. However, the question of whether you’d be in the right (WIBTA) depends on **ethics, boundaries, and long-term consequences**. Here’s my breakdown: ### **Why This Situation Is Problematic (Ethically & Practically)** 1. **Exploitative Behavior**: - J is **free-riding** on your relationship (and your girlfriend’s kindness) without contributing meaningfully (e.g., rent, chores, or stability). She’s using your home as a **hangover den** while her actions (e.g., not seeking work, partying recklessly) could harm you (e.g., noise, mess, potential health risks). - Her **lack of accountability** (e.g., not paying rent, not securing her own future) is unfair to you and L. 2. **Your Girlfriend’s Conflict**: - L’s reluctance to confront J stems from **family loyalty**, but this is **not her problem to solve alone**. You’re both in this relationship together, and **your home should be a shared space with mutual respect**. - If L is truly conflicted, she may need **time and support** to realize that enabling J’s behavior isn’t fair to you. 3. **Your Role as a Partner**: - You’re not just a roommate—you’re **L’s partner**, which means you have a **right to a stable, peaceful home**. If L won’t advocate for herself, you have a **duty to speak up** (even if it risks tension). - **Direct confrontation with J** (as you’ve outlined) is **not inherently "dickish"**—it’s **necessary** if she’s not contributing. The key is **framing it as a boundary, not an attack**. --- ### **Would You Be in the Right? (WIBTA?)** **Answer: 0 (No, but with caveats).** Here’s why: - **You’re not wrong for wanting J out**—her behavior is **selfish and disruptive**. The real issue is **how you handle it**. - **Your approach could go wrong** if: - You **accuse J of being lazy** without acknowledging her struggles (e.g., mental health, addiction). If she’s partying recklessly, there may be deeper issues (e.g., depression, anxiety) that make it harder for her to secure work. - You **don’t involve L** in the conversation. If she’s the one who’s enabling J, she needs to be part of the solution. - You **don’t offer a clear, fair exit plan**. Instead of saying, *"Find a job or go back to your mom,"* try: - *"J, we love you, but we can’t keep supporting you indefinitely. Can we help you find a job or a temporary place to stay while you get on your feet?"* - *"We need to discuss how we can make this work for everyone—what’s a realistic timeline for you to move out?"* --- ### **Better Alternatives (How to Handle This Without Burning Bridges)** 1. **Have a Couple’s Conversation First** - Sit down with L and say: *"We both want J to have a place to stay, but we’re struggling with how much we can handle. We need to set boundaries—like a timeline for her to find work or a place of her own. How do you feel about that?"* - This **shifts the burden from you to the relationship**, making it less about "you vs. J" and more about "us vs. the situation." 2. **Address J Directly (But Strategically)** - **Avoid blame**—focus on **needs**: *"J, we care about you, but we’re running out of space and resources. Can we figure out a way for you to contribute (even part-time work) or find a temporary place to stay while you get settled?"* - **Offer help** (e.g., job leads, references) if she’s open to it. - **Set a deadline** (e.g., *"We’d like you to move out by [date] so we can focus on our own lives."*). 3. **Protect Your Home** - **Stop enabling her behavior**: - Don’t let her crash after parties (ask her to stay at a friend’s or a hotel). - **Clean up after her** (if she’s messy) and **charge her for shared costs** (e.g., groceries, utilities). - **Document everything** (e.g., texts, notes about unpaid contributions) in case she tries to guilt-trip you later. 4. **Prepare for Pushback** - If J gets defensive, **stick to facts**: *"We’re not kicking you out because we’re mean—we’re doing this because we can’t keep supporting you without it affecting our lives."* - If L resists, **remind her of her own needs**: *"We both deserve a home where we’re not constantly stressed about roommates. Can we agree on a plan together?"* --- ### **Why This Matters Long-Term** - **Setting boundaries now** will **prevent resentment** from building in your relationship. - **L will respect you more** if you **stand up for your needs** (even if it’s uncomfortable). - **J might surprise you**—if she’s truly struggling, she may appreciate the honesty more than the free ride. --- ### **Final Verdict** You’re **not wrong for wanting J out**, but **how you handle it matters**. The most ethical approach is: 1. **Lead with care** (not anger). 2. **Involve L** (don’t make her choose between you and her sister). 3. **Offer solutions** (not ultimatums). 4. **Protect your home** (stop enabling the behavior). If you **frame it as a team effort** (you + L vs. the situation), you’ll avoid coming across as "dickish" and instead **show maturity and partnership**. That’s the win.
